description: Every on-screen claim maps to a source here. For each, `quote` is the EXACT verbatim text in the paper that supports the claim; the capture pipeline locates that text and records its pixel rectangle (`locator`) so the video zooms to the precise sentence/figure — never a guessed spot. Claims were re-verified against primary sources (see CORRECTIONS.md).

sources.claim: Self-reported feeling needed 27 distinct emotion categories — bridged by smooth gradients, contrary to basic-emotion theories.
sources.stat: 853 participants rated 2,185 emotional videos; 27 categories emerged.
sources.citation: Cowen, A. S., & Keltner, D. (2017). Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients. PNAS, 114(38), E7900–E7909.
sources.quote: 27 distinct varieties of reported emotional experience
sources.license: Free to read via PMC; shown as fair-use educational commentary (PNAS is not CC-BY).

sources.claim: People who finely distinguish their negative emotions regulate them better — especially as the feeling gets more intense.
sources.stat: N=53; negative-emotion differentiation predicted more regulation, particularly at higher intensity.
sources.citation: Barrett, L. F., Gross, J., Christensen, T. C., & Benvenuto, M. (2001). Knowing what you're feeling and knowing what to do about it. Cognition & Emotion, 15(6), 713–724.
sources.quote: particularly at higher levels of emotional intensity
sources.license: Author-hosted PDF (Barrett lab); fair-use academic commentary (Cognition & Emotion is subscription).

sources.claim: People skilled at naming their negative feelings used nearly 30% more strategies to regulate them over two weeks.
sources.stat: ~30% more regulation strategies (Kashdan et al.'s summary of Barrett 2001).
sources.citation: Kashdan, T. B., Barrett, L. F., & McKnight, P. E. (2015). Unpacking emotion differentiation. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 24(1), 10–16.

sources.claim: Low emotional granularity carries real costs: people high in granularity were 20–50% less likely to retaliate aggressively.
sources.stat: 20–50% less likely to retaliate; ~40% less alcohol when stressed; less insula/ACC activity when rejected.
sources.citation: Kashdan, T. B., Barrett, L. F., & McKnight, P. E. (2015). Unpacking emotion differentiation. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 24(1), 10–16.

sources.claim: Emotional granularity is trainable — it measurably increased after two weeks of tracking feelings in the moment.
sources.stat: Granularity rose with a medium effect (positive d=0.50, negative d=0.32).
sources.citation: Hoemann, K., Barrett, L. F., & Quigley, K. S. (2021). Emotional granularity increases with intensive ambulatory assessment. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 704125.
sources.quote: emotional granularity increased over the course of ambulatory assessment
sources.license: CC-BY — may be reproduced with attribution.

sources.claim: Some people genuinely can't name their feelings — a trait called alexithymia — and it's more common than you'd think.
sources.stat: In 1,285 Finnish adults: 13% overall; men 17%, women 10%.
sources.citation: Salminen, J. K., et al. (1999). Prevalence of alexithymia and its association with sociodemographic variables in the general population of Finland. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 46(1), 75–82.
sources.license: Subscription journal (Elsevier); NCBI/PubMed bot-gates headless capture, so shown as a citation card (no screenshot).

sources.claim: Just putting a feeling into words — 'affect labeling' — calms the amygdala, the brain's threat alarm.
sources.stat: Affect labeling reduced amygdala activity (t(29)=2.14, d=0.79) and raised right VLPFC activity.
sources.citation: Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.
sources.quote: the response of the amygdala and other limbic regions
sources.license: Author-hosted PDF (University of Oregon); fair-use academic commentary.

sources.claim: Naming a feeling works as 'implicit' emotion regulation — it calms you without even feeling like effort.
sources.stat: Affect labeling attenuates emotional experience, unlike effortful techniques.
sources.citation: Torre, J. B., & Lieberman, M. D. (2018). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling as implicit emotion regulation. Emotion Review, 10(2), 116–124.

sources.claim: Across 2,474 languages, emotion words differ by culture — yet are universally organized by good-vs-bad and calm-vs-activated.
sources.stat: 2,474 languages analyzed via 'colexification'; universal axes: valence + physiological activation.
sources.citation: Jackson, J. C., et al. (2019). Emotion semantics show both cultural variation and universal structure. Science, 366(6472), 1517–1522.

sources.claim: Other languages have named feelings English never did — a scholar catalogued 216 'untranslatable' well-being words.
sources.stat: A quasi-systematic search found 216 untranslatable words (now 1,000+).
sources.citation: Lomas, T. (2016). Towards a positive cross-cultural lexicography: Enriching our emotional landscape through 216 'untranslatable' words pertaining to well-being. The Journal of Positive Psychology, 11(5), 546–558.
sources.quote: A quasi-systematic search uncovered 216 such terms
sources.license: Subscription journal; cited on screen (no screenshot). Author open-access copy: roar.uel.ac.uk/4744/

sources.claim: That warm, teary feeling when people suddenly connect has a scientific name — kama muta — and it's cross-cultural.
sources.stat: Studied in 19 nations, 5 continents, 15 languages, 3,542 participants; warmth in chest, tears, chills.
sources.citation: Zickfeld, J. H., et al. (2019). Kama muta: Conceptualizing and measuring the experience often labelled being moved across 19 nations and 15 languages. Emotion, 19(3), 402–424.
sources.license: Author preprint PDF; fair-use academic commentary.

sources.claim: The chills a song gives you are physically real — skin and heart-rate sensors spike at the exact 'chill' moment.
sources.stat: N=95; skin conductance and heart rate peaked during chill episodes.
sources.citation: Grewe, O., Nagel, F., Kopiez, R., & Altenmüller, E. (2009). Chills as an indicator of individual emotional peaks. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1169, 351–354.

sources.claim: People high in the personality trait 'Openness' get these musical chills more often.
sources.stat: N=100; frisson frequency correlated with Openness to Experience.
sources.citation: Colver, M. C., & El-Alayli, A. (2016). Getting aesthetic chills from music: The connection between openness to experience and frisson. Psychology of Music, 44(3), 413–427.
sources.quote: frequency of frisson was positively correlated with overall Openness to Experience
sources.license: Subscription journal; cited on screen (no screenshot).

sources.claim: Awe — feeling tiny before something vast — is defined by two things: perceived vastness and a need to update your mind.
sources.stat: Two central appraisals of awe: perceived vastness + need for accommodation.
sources.citation: Keltner, D., & Haidt, J. (2003). Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion. Cognition & Emotion, 17(2), 297–314.
sources.quote: perceived vastness, and a need for accommodation
sources.license: Author-hosted PDF (Greater Good, UC Berkeley); fair-use academic commentary.

sources.claim: In experiments, awe shrinks the self — the 'small self' — and makes people more generous.
sources.stat: 5 studies, N=2,078; awe → 'small self' → more prosocial behavior.
sources.citation: Piff, P. K., Dietze, P., Feinberg, M., Stancato, D. M., & Keltner, D. (2015). Awe, the small self, and prosocial behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 108(6), 883–899.
sources.license: Subscription journal (APA); cited on screen (no screenshot).

folkloreDoNotCiteAsScience.term: Sonder & The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows (John Koenig)
folkloreDoNotCiteAsScience.note: Poetic neologisms, NOT peer-reviewed. If used, label clearly as coined words and credit Koenig — never present as research.

corrections: Barrett 2001 does NOT contain the '30% more strategies' figure — that is Kashdan et al. 2015's paraphrase (now cited as kashdan-2015-strategies).
Harrison & Loui 2014 is a review and was REMOVED as the source for chills physiology/Openness; physiology now cited to Grewe et al. 2009, Openness to Colver & El-Alayli 2016.
'Small self' is Piff et al. 2015, not Keltner & Haidt 2003 (which gives vastness + need for accommodation).
